title.title: Subset Sum in $O(2^{0.49n})$ time
title.subtitle: Claim: worst-case Subset Sum on $n$ integers in $O(2^{0.49n})$ randomized time, below meet-in-the-middle

plain: Pick numbers from a list that add up to a target: the half-century-old split-in-half method is beaten

panels.caption: pick numbers that hit a target exactly, here $7 + 8$

beats.text: Subset Sum: is there a subset of $n$ integers with exactly the target sum?
Worst case: $2^{n/2}$ since Horowitz and Sahni in 1974
Claimed: $2^{0.49n}$. Small, but the first exponential dent in 50 years

steps: Random tie-breaks leave at most one exact solution
If there are few distinct sums, split and match
Otherwise, add random spins over near hits
Subtract the false hits; what's left says yes or no

after.label: Claimed, 4 Oct 2026
after.note: randomized, success at least $2/3$, word RAM

achievement.note: The saving is $2^{0.01n}$: a factor of two at $n = 100$

verify.ourCheck: We did not referee the proof; nothing here is machine-checked

voice.text: Split the list in half and match: the record since nineteen seventy four.
Random spins over near hits, minus the false ones, reveal a solution.
Claimed: two to the point four nine n.

sources.quote: A uniform randomized algorithm solves worst-case Subset Sum on n polynomial-bit integers in O(2^{0.49n}) word-RAM time on every execution (intermediate bound 2^{0.489995n} poly), success >= 2/3.
The saving is $2^{0.01n}$, so at $n = 100$ it is a factor of two
A worst-case 2^{0.49n} would break a 50-year barrier
